survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This brief uses PIRLS trend data across four cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016) for fourth graders and their parents, focusing on two questionnaire-based attitude scales (“students like reading” and “parents like reading”). The analysis constructs scale scores by summing unchanged questionnaire items across cycles (students’ scale: 3 items scored 0–9; parents’ scale: 4 items scored 0–12) and then computes country mean scale scores for each cycle. The brief does not report the use of PIRLS sampling weights or replicate weights, nor any specific weight variable names, so the weighting approach is not documented in the provided text. Because the study is a descriptive trend analysis of mean scale scores (not an ML model), the manuscript does not specify any additional preprocessing beyond item scoring, reverse-coding, and restricting the sample to countries with trend participation and (for parents) countries that administered the parent questionnaire.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are questionnaire-based attitude scale scores derived from summed Likert-type items (“students like reading” and “parents like reading”), not cognitive achievement scores with PIRLS plausible values. As a result, plausible values handling is not applicable to these attitude measures. The brief also does not document a missing-data strategy for questionnaire nonresponse or item nonresponse (e.g., complete-case vs imputation), so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Trend analysis uses PIRLS fourth-grade questionnaire items that remained unchanged across the four PIRLS cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016). The brief restricts the trend sample to the 18 countries (plus two benchmarking participants: Ontario and Quebec) that participated in all four cycles. For “students like reading,” results are reported for all participating countries; for “parents like reading,” results are not reported for England and the United States because those countries did not administer the parents’ questionnaire. The brief also reverse-codes specific items (e.g., “I think reading is boring” and “I read only if I have to/need information”) and then sums item scores to form the two scale scores; it does not specify additional exclusions beyond the country participation and questionnaire administration restrictions.

data.outcome_summary: This IEA brief reports descriptive international trends in reading attitudes among fourth graders and their parents using PIRLS questionnaire data collected in 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016. It constructs two scale scores from questionnaire items that remained unchanged across cycles: “students like reading” (three items summed to a 0–9 scale) and “parents like reading” (four items summed to a 0–12 scale). Across the 18 countries participating in all cycles (plus Ontario and Quebec as benchmarking participants), students’ “like reading” scores declined in most countries between 2001 and 2016, with only England and Iran showing increases; between 2011 and 2016, no country showed an increase. Parents’ “like reading” scores also declined in most countries between 2001 and 2016 and between 2006 and 2016, with no increases between 2011 and 2016. The brief emphasizes that these are trend descriptions and do not establish causal explanations for the declines, and it does not document a missing-data handling strategy for questionnaire nonresponse in the provided text.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a descriptive trend brief rather than an empirical ML study: it reports mean changes over time in questionnaire-derived attitude scales and does not train or evaluate predictive models. Consequently, fields related to ML techniques, PV handling, and missing-data handling are either not applicable (no PV-based achievement outcomes) or not reported (no explicit missing-data protocol is described in the provided text). The absence of student-level sample sizes and weighting details is consistent with a policy brief format that focuses on cross-cycle descriptive comparisons rather than inferential modeling.
